newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: "Quant" to head SBC private banking.
newsitem.headline: "Quant" to head SBC private banking.

text.p: Swiss Bank Corp has underscored its aim to bring quantitative analytics to the fore in its business by naming Rodolfo Bogni -- a man flattered to be called a "quant" -- chief executive of its private banking division.

Bankers say the expertise of quantitative analysts, or "quants," is increasingly in demand as financial practitioners harness sophisticated computer models for risk management and accounting or to enhance returns.

"I would say that the quantitative aspects of finance pervade every aspect of banking, including private banking, because the clientele has become extremely sophisticated," Bogni, set to take over on July 1, told Reuters.

Bogni joined SBC in 1990 as chief executive of SBC in London. From January 1996 to the end of March 1997, he took leave to study mathematics applied to options theory at the Centre of Quantitative Finance at Imperial College in London.
"Even in this business it has become extremely important to know quantitative finance not only for risk management purposes, but also for investment purposes in a more specific sense," Bogni said.
"We as an institution are not trying to change particularly the nature of private banking, it is just that the nature of investment is becoming increasingly sophisticated," he said.
"Many of the assets available for investment purposes today have either explicit or imbedded structures of a derivative nature," he said.

Often a distinction is made between linear-type analysis, which is considered more mainstream and uses relatively familiar mathematical equations, and non-linear, which looks for patterns in what may appear to be random events.
Bogni suggested SBC would probably use a more linear approach.

"Our models are mostly linear. It all boils down to the use of partial differential equations and stochastic calculus. The domain of finance is still a rather narrow one from a mathematical viewpoint," said Bogni.
No matter what his mathematical leanings, the appointment was viewed as something of a revolution in Zurich.
"Electing someone of his calibre, who goes off and takes a sabbatical, that is a profound move," said Richard Olsen, chairman of financial firm Olsen and Associates in Zurich.
Due to the hierarchical nature of Swiss banks, Bogni's appointment may have a bigger impact than would be the case in a similar situation in the U.S., he added.

"He will have more leverage in his institution. The whole company is structured in a hierarchical fashion. When he takes over and says 'Look what I learned there' --if they suddenly adopt this approach -- then they can be effective," Olsen said.
SBC got a push in the direction of complex quantitative analysis with the 1992 acquisition of Chicago-based O'Connor & Associates, which had a 20-year history in options trading.
Banks often use derivatives, especially options, to insure against price fluctuations of securities in a portfolio.
Even simple transactions like a mortgage contain embedded options, in this case, the prepayment clause.

Options in financial transactions make it hard to evaluate their value without mathematical models to assess constantly changing variables like the price of an underlying security, volatility, time to expiry and interest rate fluctuations.
Risk management and profitability go hand in hand, according to one top expert in the business, Myron Scholes, who along with Fischer Black developed the Black-Scholes option pricing model.

"Risk management is not reducing risk, but it is trying to say what risks do I want to take, and what risks do I not want to take," Scholes said in a recent talk at the Swiss-American Chamber of Commerce.
One could also turn the concept around into what would be "an optimisation system" to manage business in an efficient manager and optimise profits with the risks taken, he said.
